source_title: 'Controlled Implosion Of The Economy' And End Of Democracy Explained | Xueqin Jiang

interactions.summary: Jiang delivers an editorial cold-open preview: an AI-driven economic crash, popular demand for a debt-canceling king, a China-US rapprochement, and a 2028 Obama-versus-Trump showdown with Trump winning.
The host welcomes Jiang back, frames the discussion around China-US relations, the AI bubble, and digital currencies, and Jiang briefly thanks him.
The host asks whether the new Trump-Xi trade understanding marks real progress in China-US relations or just another cycle of suspended tariff threats and minor concessions.

Jiang answers that the Trump-Xi meeting signals a real turnaround and predicts a major rapprochement because the two economies remain structurally dependent on one another despite first-term hostility.
The host follows up by asking why Trump issued the threat of 100 percent tariffs if rapprochement was always the likely path.
Jiang answers that Trump's tariff threat was theater: a reality-TV style of bluster that creates conflict, draws attention, and ends in a staged resolution markets already expected.

The host pivots to China's pending fifteenth five-year plan, summarizes the early policy language around broader opening and tech modernization, and asks what Jiang expects from China's development over the next five years.
Jiang dismisses the plan rhetoric and argues that China's deeper civilizational problem is state-directed capital flowing to the politically connected rather than to the most innovative producers.
The host pushes back that China's visible successes in EVs, solar, and a vibrant tech sector suggest the model is producing real innovation.
Jiang replies that the celebrated EV success is actually overproduction driven by subsidies, forcing China to dump cheap cars abroad and damaging European industry.
The host asks what Xi ultimately wants, what Trump wants for himself and America, and whether those ambitions are on a collision course or can cooperate for the next few years.

Jiang answers with a geopolitical rule: domestic conflict is more intense than interstate conflict, so both Xi and Trump are using diplomacy to consolidate their internal power bases, with Xi chiefly seeking regime consolidation and a stable US relationship.
After a sponsor interruption, the host resumes by asking whether China truly seeks global superpower status and whether that would force a collision with the United States.

Jiang answers that the China Dream is usually misread in the West: it is mainly about sovereignty, territorial integrity, preventing Taiwan's independence, and dealing with other powers on a peer-to-peer basis rather than remaking the world.
The host asks whether deeper opening-up could destabilize China and eventually produce a democratic revolution.
Jiang rejects that scenario and says Chinese people mainly want stability and modest prosperity, not democracy or an American-style standard of living.
The host pivots to the United States, citing a Bright Line Watch survey and asking whether the claim that America is sliding toward authoritarianism has any objective truth.
The segment is an empty boundary artifact between the host's survey framing and Jiang's substantive answer, so it carries no independent interview content.

Jiang answers that the United States is already moving toward authoritarian rule because Trump entered his second term with far less internal resistance, while ICE raids, National Guard deployment, possible wars, emergency powers, and a passive Democratic opposition leave him room to consolidate power beyond normal democratic constraints.

The host pushes back by asking whether Western publics would really accept dictatorship or monarchy and what alternative political form Jiang thinks people would choose if liberal democracy breaks down.

Jiang reframes the choice as monarchy versus oligarchy, argues America has effectively been an oligarchy since the 2008 bailout era, and says debt-burdened citizens may prefer a king who promises jubilee and redistribution, making a Trump-Obama vice-presidential showdown in 2028 plausible.

Jiang finishes his monarchy-versus-oligarchy answer by predicting that a 2028 contest could effectively become Trump versus Obama even if both men appear only as vice-presidential candidates, and that Trump would win easily.
The host reacts to Jiang's 2028 forecast and asks whether a two-term president could legally run again as a vice-presidential candidate.

Jiang answers that the American system depends more on consensus, norms, and shared values than on airtight legal barriers, so an actor who ignores those norms can push beyond what the system is able to restrain.
The host pivots to the stock market, asking Jiang how he reads all-time-high equities, tech-led gains, data-center-driven GDP, and the broader AI-market story.

Jiang argues that the AI boom is a mutually financed bubble that still lacks a working profit model, drains public resources through expensive data centers, and is pushing the economy toward disaster, which makes elite-managed social unrest and a controlled implosion of the economy thinkable.
The host presses the point by asking whether the whole bubble is being engineered by tech companies or whether some other force is driving it.
Jiang answers that the AI bubble is fully engineered by tech firms through circular financing in which companies effectively lend inflated value back and forth to one another.
The host restates Jiang's point as circular financing and asks whether that self-reinforcing structure is still good for investors and the broader market in the short term.

Jiang argues that both America and China are converging on a state-planning model that misallocates capital, and he says AI creates a paradox where success destroys jobs while failure crashes the economy.
The host asks what event would actually trigger the bubble to pop.

Jiang says the pop would come through a controlled, engineered implosion in which companies, banks, and financial actors decide to cash out, and he uses 2008 plus Goldman Sachs betting against its own CDO machine as the model.
The host pushes back by noting that markets still look calm and asks whether current optimism and low volatility are actually telling the truth about the economy.

Jiang answers that market calm is just elite paralysis: institutional investors have no exit, so the whole financial system keeps speeding downhill with its eyes shut and hoping the crash does not arrive yet.
The host pivots to the GENIUS Act, stablecoins, and tokenization of real-world assets, asking whether state-backed digital finance changes Jiang's bearish assessment.

Jiang argues that tokenization and digital currency are tools of financial repression that keep an overheated debt economy stable by obstructing bank runs, and he adds that America would need a manufactured crisis to force full adoption while he would still personally hold dollars rather than gold or crypto.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang answer with embedded host interjection in ASR

interactions.summary: The host asks whether a stablecoin-based world with self-custodied digital dollars and frictionless payments would actually improve Jiang's daily life.

Jiang says digital payments in China have made daily life easier and safer, but programmable currency also gives the state the power to freeze accounts and discipline people directly through the payment system.

Jiang finishes his digital-currency answer by arguing that convenience comes at the price of anonymity, individual agency, and a social contract that protects private economic choice from direct state control.
The host asks Jiang to end on something hopeful by naming a social or economic development that could genuinely improve living standards.

Jiang says a US-China rapprochement is the main hopeful path because Chinese goods and exported deflation could ease American inflation, and he predicts the next year will show clearer signals of the two status-quo powers moving back toward cooperation.

speaker_notes.note: The packet opens with a Jiang teaser monologue before the host introduction, suggesting the published video uses an editorial cold open rather than strict conversational chronology.
The host's trade-deal setup and the reminder about the canceled November 1 tariff operate as one continuous question split across two segments.

The host appears to read or paraphrase current policy-summary language about the fifteenth five-year plan before asking his actual question, so the long setup should be treated as host framing rather than Jiang's position.
The host's challenge about EVs, solar panels, and China's tech sector functions as a substantive pushback question rather than a separate claim block.

Segment 0019 contains a long sponsor read before the host returns to the actual interview question at the end; the ad copy is part of the source artifact but not part of Jiang's geopolitical argument.
The host quotes survey language and numbers but immediately says he has not read the details, so the cited poll functions as provisional framing rather than a fully endorsed factual claim.
Segment 0025 is blank and appears to be a transcript-boundary remainder rather than spoken material.
Jiang paraphrases Mark Milley as having reassured China that Trump was under control; that quoted reassurance is embedded inside Jiang's answer rather than being a separate speaker turn.
The 'embryonic secret police' line is presented by Jiang as speculation from unnamed observers, not as an independently verified fact claim by the host.
The host's legality question is partly conversational riffing and partly a real follow-up; it functions as a transition from Jiang's speculative 2028 scenario into a norms-versus-law answer.

Jiang explicitly says he is not an industry specialist and is summarizing what he reads in the news, so the monetization and financing claims here are presented as informed commentary rather than insider reporting.
Andrew Sorkin is invoked as a media signal inside Jiang's interpretive frame of 'predictive programming,' not as neutral expert confirmation.
The host is not disputing the mechanism so much as translating Jiang's improvised example into the cleaner phrase 'circular financing' before probing its short-term market payoff.
Jiang's answer moves quickly from AI-market dynamics to a broader civilizational claim that the United States and China now share the same state-planning path.
Jiang presents the 2008 comparison as a deliberate elite cash-out model rather than a spontaneous market failure, which frames the historical example as interpretive evidence for engineered collapse.
This focus ref is an empty carryover segment, likely an ASR boundary artifact from the end of Jiang's car-crash metaphor rather than a separate utterance.
The ASR folds a brief host-style investment question into Jiang's longer answer, but the substantive through-line remains Jiang's explanation of crisis-manufacture and his personal dollar preference.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang's answer is deliberately double-sided: he grants the convenience case from lived Chinese experience before pivoting to the coercive capacities of programmable money.

This segment contains repetitive ASR fragments, but the core speaker identity and argument are still clear: Jiang is extending his warning that digital currency centralizes power by removing anonymity from economic life.

The diarization folds the end of Jiang's geopolitical answer together with the host's follow-up about where to find his work, so this segment has to be split semantically rather than trusted as a single-speaker block.
These closing segments are routine outro material, but they still establish that the substantive interview has ended before the separate channel signoff in packet-0009.
This is conventional host call-to-action material after the interview itself has already ended, so it carries no new Jiang analysis.

claims.claim: Jiang classifies China and the United States as status quo powers, while Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Venezuela are revisionist powers that want the international order to change.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang geopolitical model stated on 2025-11-04.

claims.claim: Jiang says the United States and China ultimately benefit more from working together than from fighting each other, and he thinks both sides have learned that after years of conflict.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang diagnosis stated on 2025-11-04 about the present strategic incentives of both states.

claims.claim: Jiang tells listeners that his geopolitical analysis is best followed on his Predictive History Substack, while also naming his X account and YouTube channel.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang self-description stated on 2025-11-04 during the interview close.

signature_moments.moment: The cold open jumps straight from engineered crash to a post-democratic answer: people cry for a king.
signature_moments.source_phrase: then the people cry for a king
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It compresses Jiang's economic and political argument into one memorable escalation from market breakdown to regime transformation.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reduces China-US rapprochement to a blunt dependency formula rather than ideology or goodwill.
signature_moments.source_phrase: China needs the US market and the US needs Chinese to buy US dollars
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's core causal model for why great-power hostility will give way to renewed accommodation.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats the next year as a backstage settlement period where major disputes will be hashed out off camera.
signature_moments.source_phrase: behind the scenes, a lot of major issues will be hashed out
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows his predictive method: watch summit sequencing and structural incentives, not public rhetoric alone.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reduces Trump's tariff politics to television craft: manufacture conflict, then deliver the resolution.
signature_moments.source_phrase: create as much conflict as possible and then find a resolution
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives Jiang a reusable model for reading Trump's geopolitical moves as staged drama rather than stable doctrine.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats four thousand years of Chinese governance as one long problem of capital flowing toward proximity to power.
signature_moments.source_phrase: an inefficient allocation of capital
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is his civilizational compression of why modernization slogans and planning documents do not persuade him.

signature_moments.moment: The glamorous EV success story is flipped into a pathology of subsidized overcapacity dumped abroad.
signature_moments.source_phrase: overproduction in the system
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows Jiang's habit of re-reading celebrated industrial victories as symptoms of hidden structural distortion.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reframes great-power diplomacy as an effect of harsher internal power struggles rather than as the primary battlefield.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the conflict within nation states is always greater, more intense than the conflict between nation states
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's governing rule for reading Xi, Trump, and even US-China trade talks through domestic consolidation first.

signature_moments.moment: The China Dream gets stripped of civilizational grandeur and reduced to sovereignty, territorial integrity, and preventing Taiwan's independence.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the China Dream really is about maintaining national sovereignty, about maintaining territorial integrity
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's direct rebuttal to expansionist Western readings of Xi's doctrine.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses Chinese social desire into endurance rather than liberal aspiration: people will eat bitterness for the sake of stability.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the Chinese term is 吃苦, eat bitter
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the packet its sharpest image of why he thinks democratizing pressure remains weak inside China.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats immigration enforcement as a possible dry run for regime architecture rather than as a simple deportation campaign.
signature_moments.source_phrase: an embryonic secret police
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures his most provocative image of second-term Trumpism as institutional experimentation in authoritarian power.

signature_moments.moment: The democratic crisis is sharpened by Jiang's suggestion that the opposition is passively waiting for chaos while the very existence of future midterms becomes uncertain.
signature_moments.source_phrase: who says there will be midterms next November?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns ordinary partisan incompetence into a regime-transition warning.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang collapses the constitutional choice into a harsher binary: not monarchy or democracy, but monarchy or oligarchy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the choice isn't between monarchy and democracy, the choice is between monarchy and oligarchy
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's central reversal and the hinge that lets him move from authoritarian drift to popular desire for a king.

signature_moments.moment: The king appears as an anti-oligarchic debt canceller whose first act is jubilee.
signature_moments.source_phrase: his first act is often a Jubilee, where he cancels the debts of the people
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives Jiang's monarchy argument a concrete economic mechanism rather than leaving it as vague strongman psychology.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang shifts the constitutional edge case away from black-letter legality and toward the fragility of a system built on norms that can be ignored.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's wrong. It's immoral. It's unconventional. But it's not illegal
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is his compact formula for why formal democratic rules may fail to restrain a determined norm-breaker.

signature_moments.moment: The AI sector is pictured as a survival bubble where firms prop each other up without a real profit engine underneath.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's essentially a bubble that they have to all prop up in order to survive
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It compresses Jiang's critique of the AI economy into a vivid mechanism instead of a generic valuation complaint.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns AI exuberance into a disaster-management question: not whether the economy will fail, but whether elites can implode it in a controlled way.
signature_moments.source_phrase: can the Americans manage a controlled implosion of the economy?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That phrase carries the packet's core image of deliberate economic demolition under cover of crisis.

signature_moments.moment: Media discussion of a 1929 replay is recast as preparatory scripting for a financial event that powerful actors already expect to manage.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this sounds like predictive programming to me
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows how Jiang folds mainstream crash commentary into his broader model of engineered crisis.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns tech finance into a cartoon of elites swapping billion-dollar puppies back and forth, making the market feel absurdly self-referential.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I give you a billion dollars for a puppy
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The image compresses his claim that the bubble's valuations are circular theater rather than grounded production.

signature_moments.moment: AI becomes a no-win machine: if it fails the economy implodes, and if it works the economy implodes anyway by wiping out jobs.
signature_moments.source_phrase: If it doesn't work, the economy implodes. But if it does work, then the economy implodes.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That double-bind is the packet's sharpest statement of Jiang's anti-progress reading of the AI boom.

signature_moments.moment: The trigger for collapse is not panic from below but elites deciding together that it is time to cash out and manage the fallout.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's a controlled implosion
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's core mechanism for how bubbles end in Jiang's model: deliberate withdrawal by insiders, not innocent surprise.

signature_moments.moment: Goldman becomes the emblem of a system that profits more from detonating its own machine than from keeping the machine running.
signature_moments.source_phrase: they could make even more money betting against their own CDOs
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives Jiang a vivid historical precedent for engineered implosion as rational elite behavior.

signature_moments.moment: The financial system becomes a driver and passenger hurtling down a mountain while both keep their eyes closed and call that calm.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the driver says, well, I have my eyes closed as well
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The image compresses Jiang's claim that market composure is not confidence but shared paralysis among actors who cannot escape.

signature_moments.moment: Digital currency is stripped of its futuristic gloss and recast as a mechanism for keeping a debt-sick system alive by preventing flight.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a fancy work around the idea of financial repression
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's compact formula for the political purpose of tokenization in a failing economy.

signature_moments.moment: The road to digital currency runs through engineered emergency: America would need a manufactured crisis to make people accept it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: America needs to manufacture a crisis
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That line connects monetary digitization to Jiang's larger worldview of crisis as a governing technology.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang gives the convenience case its due and then flips it into programmable punishment: the state can simply freeze your account to teach you a lesson.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we're going to freeze this account for the next week
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's central duality that digital money is both smoother life and tighter sovereign control.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang strips away the convenience rhetoric and says digital currency means giving the government your power because anonymity has been abolished inside the economy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you've eliminated anonymity from the economy
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's sharpest formula for why programmable money matters politically rather than just technically.

signature_moments.moment: Healthy-person paternalism turns into civilizational loss: a system that can optimize your purchases can also destroy individuality itself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: that destroys the social contract
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Jiang's move from lifestyle convenience to a direct argument about the political annihilation of agency.

signature_moments.moment: His closing hope is not moral uplift but exported deflation: the best future on offer is a repaired US-China circuit that lowers the American cost of living again.
signature_moments.source_phrase: China was able to export this deflation overseas
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That line condenses Jiang's closing optimism into a concrete macroeconomic mechanism rather than a generic plea for peace.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang redraws the global board by pairing China and America as status-quo powers on one side and casting Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Venezuela as the revisionist bloc.
signature_moments.source_phrase: China and the United States are status quo powers
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's most compact geopolitical classification and explains why he expects eventual cooperation despite recent hostility.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's term for a coming improvement and normalization in China-US relations after years of posturing and hostility.
The elite bloc against which Jiang imagines a debt-canceling king could politically unify the public after an engineered crash.
The threatened Trump tariff level that frames the host's question about whether the trade confrontation was real leverage or political theater.
The current Chinese planning cycle the host uses to frame expectations about technology, opening-up, and the next five years of development.
Jiang's core diagnosis of state planning in China: capital follows political connection rather than productive energy or innovation.
Jiang's description of a subsidized production glut, especially in EVs, that forces China to export excess output abroad.
Xi-era concept Jiang reads not as a mandate for global domination but as a sovereignty-and-stability program centered on territorial integrity and domestic order.
Jiang's phrase for how China wants to negotiate with the United States and other great powers: as an equal sovereign rather than as a subordinate or ideological convert.
Rendered by Jiang as 'eat bitter'; his shorthand for a willingness to endure hardship in exchange for stability and modest prosperity.
Jiang's phrase for the suspicion that ICE is being tested as an early authoritarian enforcement apparatus rather than functioning only as an immigration agency.
Used here as shorthand for extraordinary domestic coercive authority that Jiang sees Trump publicly considering.
Jiang's name for the post-2008 American order in which economic gains and political design are geared toward the top tier rather than the general public.
Jiang's term for the king's debt-canceling first act, making monarchy legible as economic relief for indebted citizens.
Jiang's term for a deliberately managed economic crash designed to limit fallout for powerful actors rather than allow a fully uncontrolled collapse.
Jiang's phrase for public messaging that acclimates people to an outcome before it arrives, here applied to talk of a coming 1929-style crash.
Used here through subsidy-driven data-center buildout and political direction of capital rather than through a purely market allocation process.
The host's label for Jiang's description of companies inflating one another through reciprocal investment and lending rather than through productive returns.
Jiang's term for a political economy where the state and connected power centers direct capital, producing inefficient allocation and converging American and Chinese market structures.
Jiang's phrase for an engineered economic collapse managed by insiders who cash out before the wider system absorbs the damage.
Collateralized debt obligations cited by Jiang as the debt instruments around which the 2008 crisis and elite short-against-the-product behavior were organized.
Jiang's term for a regime that constrains financial behavior and transactions so indebted, overheated systems remain governable and deposit flight becomes harder.
Introduced by the host as digitizing real-world assets and then reinterpreted by Jiang as a monetary-control mechanism rather than a neutral technical upgrade.
In Jiang's usage, a payment system that makes transactions frictionless for ordinary life while also enabling financial repression and direct state supervision.
Digital money that authorities can condition or interrupt, including freezing accounts and disciplining people through the payments infrastructure.
In Jiang's usage, digital money that can be tracked, restricted, and behaviorally conditioned by the state rather than merely transferred more efficiently.
Jiang's category for states like China and the United States that benefit from keeping the broad international order in place.
Jiang's category for states like Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Venezuela that want the present order changed rather than preserved.
Jiang's phrase for China easing foreign living costs by sending lower-priced goods outward, thereby transmitting its domestic deflationary pressure into other economies.

chronology_notes.note: The published interview opens with a Jiang teaser before the host introduction, so the first packet contains both an editorial cold open and the start of the live conversation on 2025-11-04.

Jiang explicitly contrasts the first Trump term's hostility with the second Trump term's softer atmosphere and ties his rapprochement forecast to scheduled April and December visits in the coming year.

The host situates the exchange at the moment China's fifteenth five-year plan is still being finalized and only partial recommendations are public, so Jiang's reply is a contemporaneous reaction to a rollout rather than to a finished document.

On the same 2025-11-04 date that Jiang predicts nearer-term China-US rapprochement, he also delivers a harsh long-duration critique of China's internal capital-allocation model; the packet preserves both rather than flattening them into a single pro- or anti-China stance.

On 2025-11-04 Jiang pairs his forecast of a more stable US-China relationship with a specifically domestic reading of Xi's goals, so rapprochement is framed here as a tool of regime consolidation rather than as ideological convergence.

The host dates the US-authoritarianism discussion to Trump's second term and to a post-election survey moment, anchoring Jiang's next packet response in a late-2025 American political setting rather than in a generic democracy debate.
On 2025-11-04 Jiang explicitly distinguishes Trump's first term from his second, treating the second term as a new stage marked by diminished internal restraint and growing executive experimentation.

This packet anchors Jiang's democratic-breakdown argument to two future checkpoints: uncertainty over whether normal midterms will occur next November and a speculative Trump-versus-Obama vice-presidential showdown in 2028.
On 2025-11-04 Jiang links his 2028 electoral speculation to a deeper claim that American constitutional order is now governed by eroding norms more than by enforceable legal limits.

This packet marks the interview's turn from US political-form questions into Jiang's late-2025 AI-bubble and controlled-crash diagnosis, which the next packet continues by asking what specifically would trigger the pop.

On 2025-11-04 Jiang extends his earlier packet critique of Chinese state-planning inefficiency into a broader claim that the United States is now converging toward the same model through AI finance and capital direction.
Jiang uses the 2008 crisis as a historical template for how a future AI-market break would unfold: insiders recognize unsustainability, short the system, and manage the collapse.

On 2025-11-04 Jiang extends his controlled-implosion diagnosis from AI and market structure into monetary infrastructure, arguing that digital currency is one way elites keep a fragile system stable after overheating it.

This packet links China's COVID-era transaction shift to a future American digital-currency rollout, then hands off to the next packet's closing assessment of whether any broader social improvement remains possible.

On 2025-11-04 Jiang sharpens the programmable-currency warning from the prior packet by moving from frozen accounts and convenience to a broader argument that anonymity, agency, and the social contract itself are at stake.

This closing packet returns to the US-China optimism from the opening minutes but now grounds it in inflation, deflation, and a status-quo-versus-revisionist geopolitical frame, making the hoped-for rapprochement the interview's final macroeconomic answer.
Packet-0009 is a non-substantive channel outro that cleanly marks the end of the interview transcript after Jiang's final answer and signoff.
